item.title: Provisioning Everpure Cloud Azure Native Resources with the Azure CLI
item.description: I already walked through this with Terraform , provisioning an Everpure Cloud Azure Native storage pool, volume group, and volume, then mounting it to an Azure VM over iSCSI. Not everyone wants a Terraform state file for a one-off pool, so here is the same example with nothing but the Azure CLI.

item.title: Attaching Everpure Cloud Azure Native Storage to Azure Red Hat OpenShift
item.description: Previously, I deployed an Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO) cluster with Terraform , into an existing VNet with its own dedicated subnets. That gives you a working cluster, but the persistent storage still has to come from somewhere. This time I am provisioning Everpure Cloud Azure Native volume groups for the cluster, and pulling the iSCSI connection parameters back out of the API, which is the piece this post is really about.

item.title: Mounting an Everpure Cloud Azure Native Snapshot for Recovery on Linux
item.description: Are you looking for a way to get a few files back from an Everpure Cloud Azure Native snapshot without overwriting the live volume? The portal gives you two options today: overwrite the volume group, or restore the snapshot into a brand new volume group. Overwrite is destructive, and a new volume group means a new iSCSI target to mount on the VM. What I usually want is the old copy of one volume mounted next to the current one, so I can copy back what I need and throw the copy away. So I wrote a script that does exactly that. I started with Linux, and in Part 2 I do the same thing on Windows.

item.title: Mounting an Everpure Cloud Azure Native Snapshot for Recovery on Windows
item.description: Are you running Windows VMs on Everpure Cloud Azure Native and need a few files back from a snapshot without touching the live volume? In Part 1 I cloned one volume from the latest volume group snapshot and mounted it next to the original on Linux. This time it’s Windows. The Azure side is exactly the same, the guest side is where Windows does its own thing.

item.title: Running the Everpure Cloud Azure Native VMSS Agent as a VM Application
item.description: Are you looking for a way to give every scale set instance its own Everpure Cloud Azure Native volume without running an Azure Function next to it? In Part 1 and Part 2 an orchestrator Function did the storage work while each instance called it on boot and on scale-in. This time the instance does all of it itself, and the agent that does it ships as a VM Application from an Azure Compute Gallery. I ran it on a single pool in one zone first, then across two zones with a pool in each.

item.title: Multi-AZ Scaling for Everpure Cloud Azure Native Volumes on a VMSS
item.description: Are you running a scale set across availability zones and need every instance’s volume to live in the same zone as the instance? In Part 1 every instance got its own Everpure Cloud Azure Native volume on scale-out and cleaned it up on scale-in, but it all hung off a single storage pool in a single zone. This time I spread the scale set across two zones, gave each zone its own pool, and made sure an instance only ever attaches to the pool it shares a zone with.

item.title: Auto-Provisioning Everpure Cloud Azure Native Volumes for VMSS Scale Events
item.description: Are you scaling a VMSS workload that needs its own dedicated block volume per instance, one that shows up when the instance does and disappears when it’s gone? I went looking for the obvious way to wire that up on Everpure Cloud Azure Native and ran into a design that doesn’t actually exist in Azure, then built the one that does.

item.title: Provisioning Everpure Cloud Azure Native Resources with Terraform
item.description: This post walks through a complete Terraform example that provisions an Everpure Cloud Azure Native storage pool, volume group, and volume, then automatically mounts it to an Azure VM over iSCSI.
